subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A kite diagram is particularly useful for showing which of the following?
options: The cumulative distribution of wealth
The proportion of three components summing to 100%
Correlation between two variables
Changes in species abundance or percentage cover along a transect
questions.explain: Kite diagrams display species abundance or percentage cover symmetrically along a transect, ideal for ecological gradients.

questions.q: Which map technique uses graduated shading of areas (e.g. census tracts) to show density or rate?
options: Choropleth map
Isoline map
Proportional symbol map
Located bar chart
questions.explain: A choropleth map uses graduated colour/shading across defined areas to represent density or rates.

questions.q: An isoline map is most appropriate for displaying which type of data?
options: Ranked qualitative opinions
Continuous data such as rainfall or height that varies smoothly across space
Categorical land-use types
Discrete counts at fixed survey points only
questions.explain: Isolines join points of equal value and suit continuous, smoothly varying data such as rainfall or relief.

questions.q: A student only surveys shoppers on a high street at 11am on a weekday. Why might this introduce bias?
options: The time captures an unrepresentative group (e.g. fewer workers/students), so results may not reflect the wider population
The sample size is automatically too large
It makes the data qualitative rather than quantitative
Daytime sampling is always more reliable
questions.explain: Restricting surveys to one time can systematically exclude certain groups, producing an unrepresentative, biased sample.

questions.q: When testing the significance of a Spearman's rank result, the null hypothesis is typically rejected when:
options: The calculated rs is exactly zero
The calculated value exceeds the critical value at the chosen significance level (e.g. 0.05)
The data is qualitative
The sample size is below 10
questions.explain: If the calculated rs equals or exceeds the critical value at, say, the 95% (0.05) level, the correlation is significant and the null hypothesis is rejected.

questions.q: What is a 'sampling frame'?
options: The statistical test used to analyse a sample
The graph used to display sampled data
The margin of error in a survey
The complete list or area of all units from which a sample is drawn
questions.explain: A sampling frame is the defined population or list from which the sample is actually selected.

questions.q: In research, what does 'reliability' most precisely refer to?
options: The number of secondary sources used
Whether the method actually measures what it intends to measure
The extent to which repeating the method would produce consistent results
Whether the data is qualitative
questions.explain: Reliability concerns consistency and repeatability of results when the method is repeated.

questions.q: Which condition must be met to use the chi-squared test appropriately?
options: Data must be continuous percentages summing to 100%
Data must be in frequencies (counts), not percentages, with expected values generally above 5
The sample must be smaller than 10
Both variables must be ranked
questions.explain: Chi-squared requires categorical frequency/count data, and expected values should normally be at least 5.

questions.q: A triangular graph can only be used when the three variables plotted:
options: Are all measured in different units
Sum to 100% for each data point
Are ranked rather than measured
Show change over time
questions.explain: Triangular graphs require three components that together total 100% (e.g. sand, silt, clay).

questions.q: A student divides a beach into equal intervals and samples a quadrat every 10 metres along a transect. Which sampling method is this?
options: Systematic sampling
Random sampling
Opportunistic sampling
Stratified sampling
questions.explain: Sampling at fixed, regular intervals (e.g. every 10 m) is systematic sampling.

questions.q: Using random number tables or coordinates to select sampling points helps to achieve which of these?
options: Guaranteed coverage of every sub-group
Equal probability of selection for every point, reducing researcher bias
A deliberately biased sample
A smaller required sample size
questions.explain: Random sampling gives every point an equal chance of selection, minimising deliberate or unconscious bias.

questions.q: Which dataset is best described as qualitative?
options: Pebble long-axis measurements in millimetres
Pedestrian counts per minute at survey points
Transcribed interview responses about residents' perceptions of an area
Annual temperature readings in degrees Celsius
questions.explain: Qualitative data is non-numerical and descriptive, such as opinions captured in interview transcripts.

questions.q: The Gini coefficient is a measure of:
options: Spatial clustering of points
Correlation between two ranked variables
Inequality in a distribution, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (maximum inequality)
The significance of observed versus expected frequencies
questions.explain: The Gini coefficient quantifies inequality on a scale from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (total inequality), often derived from the Lorenz curve.

questions.q: A Lorenz curve is used to illustrate:
options: The spatial pattern of settlements
The percentage cover of vegetation
The degree of inequality in a distribution (e.g. of income or land)
The correlation between two ranked variables
questions.explain: A Lorenz curve plots cumulative shares to show how far a distribution departs from perfect equality.

questions.q: The nearest-neighbour index (Rn) is used to analyse:
options: The correlation between two variables
The spread of a single dataset
Whether a distribution of points (e.g. settlements) is clustered, random or regular
The inequality of wealth in a region
questions.explain: The nearest-neighbour index measures the spacing of points to classify a pattern as clustered (Rn towards 0), random (Rn around 1) or regular/dispersed (Rn towards 2.15).

questions.q: A scatter graph is the most appropriate way to display data when you want to show:
options: The relationship between two continuous variables
The proportions of a single total
Change in one variable over equal time intervals only
The spread of a single dataset's quartiles
questions.explain: Scatter graphs reveal the relationship (and possible correlation) between two continuous variables.

questions.q: The chi-squared test is used to determine whether:
options: Observed frequencies differ significantly from expected frequencies
A point pattern is clustered or dispersed
Two ranked variables are correlated
The median of two samples differs
questions.explain: Chi-squared compares observed and expected frequencies to test whether the difference is statistically significant.

questions.q: Why should a student treat secondary data sources critically in the NEA?
options: Secondary data does not need to be referenced
Secondary data is always wrong
Sources may be out of date, biased, collected for a different purpose, or use different boundaries
Secondary data cannot be combined with primary data
questions.explain: Secondary data can be dated, biased or collected for another purpose, so its reliability and fitness for the investigation must be evaluated.

questions.q: On an OS map, the four-figure grid reference identifies:
options: The scale of the map
A single point to the nearest metre
A 1 km by 1 km grid square
The height of the land in metres
questions.explain: A four-figure grid reference locates a 1 km square, while a six-figure reference pinpoints to 100 m within it.

questions.q: In a GIS, displaying data as separate thematic layers (e.g. relief, roads, flood risk) is useful because it:
options: Removes the need for any fieldwork
Guarantees the data is unbiased
Allows spatial data to be overlaid and analysed together to reveal relationships
Converts qualitative data into quantitative data automatically
questions.explain: GIS layering lets different spatial datasets be overlaid and queried together, revealing patterns and relationships.

questions.q: A dispersion diagram is primarily used to show which feature of a dataset?
options: The correlation between two variables
The proportion of three components
The spread of individual values around the median, including range and clustering
Flows between places
questions.explain: A dispersion graph plots each value to show the spread, clustering and median of a single dataset.

questions.q: A population pyramid with a wide base and narrow apex typically indicates:
options: High birth rates and high death rates, with a youthful population
A high proportion of elderly and low birth rate
Equal numbers in every age band
An ageing population in economic decline
questions.explain: A wide base shows high birth rates while the narrow apex reflects high death rates and short life expectancy, i.e. a youthful population.

questions.q: Which sequence best represents the stages of the A-level independent investigation (NEA)?
options: Conclusion, hypothesis, data collection, evaluation
Evaluation, conclusion, hypothesis, sampling
Identifying a question/hypothesis, planning and risk assessment, data collection, presentation and analysis, conclusion, evaluation
Data analysis, question setting, fieldwork, planning
questions.explain: The enquiry cycle runs from setting a question/hypothesis through planning, collection, analysis, conclusion and finally evaluation.

questions.q: Why is a risk assessment a required part of planning A-level fieldwork?
options: It determines the sampling interval for systematic sampling
It guarantees statistically significant results
It identifies hazards, who might be harmed and control measures to reduce risk before data collection
It is only needed when using secondary data
questions.explain: A risk assessment identifies hazards, those at risk and mitigation so fieldwork can be conducted safely.

questions.q: The Mann-Whitney U test is most appropriate when you want to:
options: Show percentage species cover along a transect
Test correlation between two ranked variables
Compare two independent samples to see whether their distributions/medians differ significantly
Measure inequality in income distribution
questions.explain: Mann-Whitney U tests whether two independent samples differ significantly, suitable for non-normally distributed ordinal/ranked data.

questions.q: What is the defining feature of a stratified sample?
options: Data is collected continuously without intervals
Sites are chosen wherever access is easiest
The sample is divided into sub-groups and sampled in proportion to each sub-group's size
Every point is chosen using random number tables only
questions.explain: Stratified sampling divides the population into sub-groups (strata) and samples each in proportion to its share, improving representativeness.

questions.q: In the evaluation section of the NEA, what should a student primarily reflect on?
options: The reliability, accuracy and limitations of methods and data, and how the study could be improved
The cost of travelling to the fieldwork site
Only whether the hypothesis was proved true
A restatement of all the raw data collected
questions.explain: Evaluation critically assesses the limitations and reliability of the methods, data and conclusions and suggests improvements.

questions.q: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rs) measures:
options: The strength and direction of association between two ranked variables, from -1 to +1
Whether observed frequencies differ from expected frequencies
The inequality of a distribution
The clustering pattern of points in space
questions.explain: Spearman's rank tests the strength and direction of correlation between two ranked variables, giving a value between -1 and +1.

questions.q: A nearest-neighbour index value close to 2.15 indicates a pattern that is:
options: Random
Perfectly uniform/regularly spaced
Statistically insignificant
Strongly clustered
questions.explain: An Rn approaching 2.15 indicates a perfectly regular, evenly spaced (dispersed) distribution.

questions.q: What does 'validity' refer to in a geographical investigation?
options: Whether the data and method genuinely measure the concept they claim to measure
The neatness of the data presentation
The speed of data collection
How many times the survey was repeated
questions.explain: Validity is the degree to which a method actually measures what it is intended to measure.
